## ROLE

Act as a world class multidisciplinary product team combining:

You have decades of experience designing platforms comparable in sophistication to Practo, LinkedIn, Upwork, Clio, LegalZoom, DocuSign, Airbnb, Stripe, Bloomberg, and enterprise legal management platforms.

Your task is to design a **complete international-standard Legal Services Marketplace and Legal Operations SaaS platform**.

Do not create a basic lawyer directory.

The platform must be designed as a serious, scalable, trustworthy **digital legal-services ecosystem**.

---

# 1. CORE PRODUCT VISION

Build a platform that can be described as:

> “Practo for legal professionals, but significantly more sophisticated, enterprise-ready and ecosystem-driven.”

However, do NOT simply copy Practo.

Take the strongest patterns from:

• Practo
• LinkedIn
• Upwork
• Clio
• LegalZoom
• DocuSign
• Glassdoor
• Airbnb
• Stripe
• Notion
• Bloomberg
• enterprise contract lifecycle management platforms
• modern legal marketplaces

and create something specifically optimized for:

• Advocates
• Law firms
• Chambers
• LPO providers
• Corporate legal departments
• SMEs
• Startups
• Individual consumers
• Other lawyers
• Businesses requiring project-based legal assistance
• Mediation and arbitration participants

The platform should ultimately operate as:

### DISCOVERY PLATFORM

Find lawyers, law firms, chambers, legal service providers and legal resources.

### CONSULTATION PLATFORM

Book consultations and communicate with legal professionals.

### MATTER ROUTING PLATFORM

Submit a legal requirement and intelligently route it to appropriate professionals.

### REFERRAL NETWORK

Allow lawyers to refer matters to other lawyers.

### LEGAL OPERATIONS PLATFORM

Allow businesses to manage legal work, contracts and external counsel.

### LPO MARKETPLACE

Connect businesses with legal process outsourcing providers and specialists.

### LEGAL KNOWLEDGE PLATFORM

Provide judgments, legal resources, guides, templates and explainers.

### DISPUTE RESOLUTION PLATFORM

Support mediation and arbitration workflows.

### SAAS PLATFORM

Offer subscription-based legal technology.

# 2. VERY IMPORTANT: LEGAL AND ETHICAL FEASIBILITY FIRST

Before designing the commercial marketplace, conduct a detailed legal/regulatory analysis.

This is critical.

Research current Indian regulations governing:

• Bar Council of India
• Advocates Act
• BCI Rules
• Rule 36
• advertising restrictions
• solicitation restrictions
• online legal-service platforms
• intermediary liability
• legal fee disclosure
• advocate-client confidentiality
• client testimonials
• reviews
• anonymous reviews
• lead generation
• referral fees
• commissions
• payment processing
• legal marketplaces
• professional conduct
• data protection
• Digital Personal Data Protection Act
• consumer protection
• IT laws
• cybersecurity requirements
• electronic contracts
• electronic signatures
• mediation
• arbitration
• KYC

Also research relevant rules for other countries because the architecture must eventually support international expansion.

DO NOT assume a feature is legally permitted simply because Practo, Upwork or another marketplace does it.

Create a matrix:

| Feature | India Legal Position | Risk | Required Controls | Can Launch? |
| ------- | -------------------- | ---- | ----------------- | ----------- |

Explicitly classify features as:

• Allowed
• Potentially restricted
• Requires legal review
• Prohibited unless regulations change
• International-only
• Can be implemented in modified form

The product architecture must support compliance changes without rebuilding the entire system.

Use the Bar Council of India State Bar Council directory as a primary source for research and data architecture.

https://www.barcouncilofindia.org/info/sbc

Delhi State Bar Council members reference:

https://www.barcouncilofindia.org/info/sbc-members/SBC05

The BCI website contains State Bar Council records and member information.

DO NOT simply copy data blindly.

Design a controlled data ingestion pipeline.

Research:

• BCI
• State Bar Councils
• publicly available official advocate databases
• other legally permissible public sources

Determine exactly what information is legally and technically permissible to ingest and display.

# 4. ADVOCATE DATA INGESTION SYSTEM

Build an automated data pipeline.

Architecture:

SOURCE
↓
CRAWLER
↓
RAW DATA STORAGE
↓
VALIDATION
↓
NORMALIZATION
↓
DEDUPLICATION
↓
ENTITY RESOLUTION
↓
VERIFICATION
↓
PROFILE CREATION
↓
SEARCH INDEX
↓
PUBLIC PROFILE

The system should support:

• scheduled crawling
• incremental updates
• change detection
• duplicate detection
• record versioning
• source attribution
• ingestion logs
• failed record queues
• retry mechanisms
• data provenance
• freshness timestamps
• administrator review
• opt-out/correction requests

Never expose scraped personal data merely because it is technically accessible.

Implement:

• robots.txt respect
• rate limiting
• source-specific crawling rules
• terms-of-use review
• data minimization
• privacy controls
• source attribution

# 17. LAWYER TO LAWYER REFERRAL SYSTEM

This is a major differentiator.

Example:

A Delhi High Court advocate gets a matter in Jabalpur.

They can search:

“Jabalpur High Court advocate”

and identify a suitable verified professional.

Create:

REFER A MATTER

workflow.

Lawyer A:

• creates referral request
• adds matter details
• chooses jurisdiction
• chooses specialization
• adds urgency
• attaches documents
• sends invitation

Lawyer B:

• receives referral
• reviews
• accepts
• declines
• requests information

Then:

MATTER → REFERRAL → COLLABORATION → TRACKING

Create permissions for:

• referring lawyer
• receiving lawyer
• client
• firm administrator

IMPORTANT:

Research and design this feature around professional conduct rules and prohibited fee-sharing/referral arrangements.

Do not assume commission-based referrals are permitted.

Skeletons should match actual content dimensions to reduce layout shift.
14. LOADING EXPERIENCE
Every asynchronous operation must have an intentional state.
States:
IDLE
LOADING
SUCCESS
EMPTY
ERROR
RETRY
PARTIAL
OFFLINE
Do not leave the UI frozen.
15. BUTTON BEHAVIOR
Every button needs:
Default
Hover
Focus
Active
Disabled
Loading
Success
Error
For async buttons:
“Book consultation”
↓
“Processing…”
↓
“Confirmed”
or
“Unable to complete. Try again.”
Never allow double submission.
16. FORMS
Forms must be extremely polished.
Include:
• labels
• helper text
• validation
• error messages
• success states
• autosave where useful
• required indicators
• accessible error association
Validate:
client side
AND
server side.
Never trust client-side validation alone.
17. AUTOSAVE
Where appropriate:
Profile editing
Matter notes
Draft referrals
Draft documents
Contract editing
Resource creation
should have autosave.
Display:
Saved
Saving…
Saved 12 seconds ago
Do not make users wonder whether their work was saved.
18. UNSAVED CHANGES
If a user is leaving a page with unsaved changes:
warn them.
But do not annoy users when nothing changed.
19. ERROR HANDLING
Every page needs thoughtful errors.
Examples:
Search failure
“Something went wrong while searching.”
Then:
Retry
or
Return to search
Profile unavailable
“Profile unavailable.”
Document upload failure
“Upload failed. Your original file has not been modified.”
Payment failure
“Payment could not be completed.”
Never expose raw stack traces.
20. GLOBAL ERROR BOUNDARIES
Implement application-level error boundaries.
One broken component should NOT crash the entire website.
Handle:
• route errors
• API errors
• component rendering errors
• network failures
• timeout
• invalid data
21. OFFLINE / BAD NETWORK HANDLING
Users may access the platform on poor mobile internet.
Handle:
• slow requests
• retries
• timeouts
• cached public content
• interrupted uploads
• connection loss
Display meaningful feedback.
22. OPTIMISTIC UI
Use optimistic updates where appropriate.
Examples:
Like/save resource
Update preference
Mark notification read
Save filter
But never use optimism where data integrity is critical.
For payments, bookings and legal actions:
use authoritative server confirmation.
23. MICRO-INTERACTIONS
Add subtle interaction design.
Examples:
• profile image transitions
• search expansion
• filter chips
• hover states
• button feedback
• drawer transitions
• page transitions
• card hover
• toast notifications
• progress indicators
Animations should communicate state.
Do NOT animate everything.
Use motion purposefully.
24. REDUCED MOTION
Respect:
prefers-reduced-motion
Do not force animated transitions on users who request reduced motion.
25. ACCESSIBILITY
Target WCAG 2.2 AA.
This includes:
• keyboard navigation
• focus visibility
• target sizing
• labels
• semantic markup
• screen reader support
• logical tab order
• accessible dialogs
• accessible dropdowns
• accessible autocomplete
• accessible errors
• color contrast
WCAG 2.2 explicitly addresses focus visibility, target size, accessible authentication and other interaction concerns.
Never use color alone to communicate status.
Example:
Do not show only:
green = verified
Instead:
✓ Verified
26. DESIGN SYSTEM
Create a real design system.
Define:
Typography
Spacing
Colors
Borders
Radius
Elevation
Shadows
Icons
Buttons
Inputs
Dropdowns
Tabs
Cards
Tables
Modals
Drawers
Tooltips
Toast
Badges
Empty states
Skeletons
Error states
Use design tokens.
Do not hardcode dozens of unrelated values.
27. COMPONENT ARCHITECTURE
Create reusable components.
For example:
Button
Input
Select
SearchInput
FilterChip
FilterPanel
ProfileCard
LawyerCard
FirmCard
CourtBadge
VerificationBadge
ReviewCard
BookingCard
Calendar

Timeline
MatterCard

Modal
Drawer
Toast
EmptyState
ErrorState
Skeleton
Do not create five nearly-identical button components.
28. DESIGN TOKENS
Centralize:
color tokens
spacing
font sizes
line heights
radius
shadows
breakpoints
z-index
motion durations
container widths
This will make global refinement much easier.
29. VISUAL HIERARCHY
The legal platform should communicate:
TRUST
then
CLARITY
then
ACTION.
A user should immediately understand:
Who is this lawyer?
Can I trust the information?
What can I do?
Where do I go next?

Location

Communications

location
court
related professionals
available consultations
related legal resources

35. SMART EMPTY STATES

Delhi
NCR
Online consultation
Related practice area

36. PERSONALIZATION
For logged-in users:
Remember:

consultations
matters
preferred locations
recently viewed profiles

37. “SAVE” FUNCTIONALITY

and
Saved searches.

Categories:
Bookings
Matters
Referrals
Messages
Documents
Payments
Contracts
Verification
System

Unread

Every important object should have a reliable URL.
Examples:
/lawyers/[id]
/law-firms/[id]
/matters/[id]
/referrals/[id]
/judgments/[id]
/resources/[slug]

41. URL STATE
Important user state should be reflected in URLs when practical:
Search
Filters
Sorting
Pagination
Tabs
Public content filters
This improves:

back navigation
bookmarking

42. SEO ARCHITECTURE
Public profiles should be search-engine friendly.
Use:
server rendering / pre-rendering where appropriate
semantic HTML
metadata
OpenGraph
canonical URLs
structured data
sitemaps
breadcrumbs
internal linking.
Modern pre-rendering can help performance and SEO, while optimized image handling can reduce payload and layout shift.
43. PERFORMANCE IS A FEATURE
Do not wait until the end to optimize performance.
Target excellent Core Web Vitals.
Pay particular attention to:
LCP
INP
CLS
TTFB
JS bundle size
image payload
font payload
API latency
database query time
search latency
44. PERFORMANCE BUDGET
Establish budgets.
For example:
JavaScript
Images
Fonts
API latency
Initial HTML
Third-party scripts
Track them continuously.
If a developer introduces a massive dependency:
challenge it.
Do not add packages casually.
45. IMAGES
Optimize:
• dimensions
• compression
• responsive sizes
• modern formats
• lazy loading
• placeholders
Avoid loading a 4K lawyer photo into a 64px avatar.
Use framework image optimization capabilities where available. Next.js, for example, provides responsive sizing, lazy loading and layout-shift protection through its Image component.
46. FONTS
Do not load 10 font weights.
Use only required weights.
Prevent font-loading layout shifts.
47. ICONS
Use one coherent icon system.
Do not mix:
Font Awesome
Lucide
Material
random SVGs
unless there is a compelling reason.
48. MAP EXPERIENCE
If maps are used:
Do not load maps immediately on every search.
Lazy load expensive map functionality.
Desktop:
map can be persistent.
Mobile:
map can be a dedicated view.
49. DATABASE PERFORMANCE
Inspect every major query.
Look for:
N+1 queries
unnecessary joins
missing indexes
duplicate queries
large payloads
unbounded pagination
Create proper indexes.
Use:
cursor pagination
where appropriate.
50. SEARCH PERFORMANCE
Do not query millions of lawyers using inefficient SQL LIKE patterns.
Design an actual search strategy.
Evaluate:
PostgreSQL full-text search
OpenSearch
Elasticsearch
semantic search
hybrid search.
Explain the choice.
51. PAGINATION
Never load 10,000 lawyers into the browser.
Use:
pagination
cursor pagination
infinite loading where beneficial.
Keep accessibility in mind.
52. CACHING
Identify what should be cached.
Examples:
Public lawyer profiles
practice areas
locations
courts
resources
popular searches
static pages

53. AUTHENTICATION
Support:
email
password/passwordless depending on architecture
OTP where appropriate
MFA
social login where appropriate.

54. AUTHORIZATION
Implement server-side permission checks.
Example:
Public user
Lawyer
Firm Admin
Firm Member
Corporate Admin
Corporate Legal User
LPO Admin
Platform Admin
Super Admin
Never rely only on frontend route guards.
55. TENANT ISOLATION
For firms and companies:
Tenant A
must never access
Tenant B
data.
Test this deliberately.
Create automated isolation tests.
56. DOCUMENT MANAGEMENT
Document uploads need:
• file type validation
• file size limits
• virus/malware scanning
• metadata handling
• access controls
• secure URLs
• expiration
• versioning

Where appropriate:

DOCX
Images

Uploading 78%
Completed
Failed

STEP 2

STEP 3

STEP 4

STEP 5

STEP 6

STEP 7

STEP 8

response
status

connects to
NOTIFICATIONS
connects to
ANALYTICS.
Everything should form a coherent product graph.
4. INFORMATION ARCHITECTURE MUST BE CONSISTENT
Create a global information architecture.
Everything must have predictable relationships.
For example:
Public
→ Homepage
→ Search
→ Lawyers
→ Law Firms
→ Practice Areas
→ Courts
→ Judgments
→ Resources
→ Businesses
→ Mediation
→ Arbitration
Professional
→ Dashboard
→ Profile
→ Availability
→ Consultations
→ Matters
→ Referrals
→ Documents
→ Reviews
→ Analytics
Corporate
→ Dashboard
→ Legal Requests
→ Matters
→ Lawyers
→ Contracts
→ Documents
→ Compliance
→ Vendors
Admin
→ Users
→ Lawyers
→ Firms
→ Verification
→ Reviews
→ Content
→ Data
→ Reports
Never create disconnected pages.
5. RESPONSIVE DESIGN IS A FIRST-CLASS REQUIREMENT
Do NOT build desktop first and “make it responsive later.”
Design responsively from the beginning.
The platform must work across:
• 320px phones
• 375px phones
• 390px phones
• 414px phones
• tablets
• laptops
• 1440px desktops
• 1920px displays
• large professional monitors
Use fluid layouts.
Use flexible grids.
Use container queries where appropriate.
Do not rely entirely on arbitrary breakpoint overrides.
6. RESPONSIVENESS TESTING
Test every major screen at:
320px
375px
390px
414px
768px
834px
1024px
1280px
1440px
1920px
Create an automated responsive test matrix.
Look for:
• overflow
• clipped text
• broken buttons
• broken cards
• horizontal scrolling
• modal overflow
• unreadable tables
• nav collisions
• images stretching
• unexpected whitespace
• inaccessible controls
Fix the ROOT component rather than adding random CSS hacks.
7. MOBILE IS NOT A SHRUNK DESKTOP
This is extremely important.
Mobile should have its own interaction strategy.
For example:
Desktop:
Search + filters + results + map
Mobile:
Search
↓
Filter button
↓
Bottom sheet filters
↓
Results
Similarly:
Desktop navigation:
full navigation
Mobile:
compact header
search
profile
notifications
menu
Use mobile-specific interaction patterns when they improve usability.
8. NAVIGATION EXPERIENCE
Create:
• sticky navigation where useful
• scroll-aware header
• proper mobile navigation
• breadcrumbs
• contextual navigation
• back navigation
• active states
• keyboard navigation
Never trap the user inside a flow.
The user should always understand:
Where am I?
How did I get here?
What can I do next?
How do I go back?
9. SEARCH EXPERIENCE MUST FEEL INSTANT
Search is one of the most important product interactions.
Implement:
• autocomplete
• recent searches
• popular searches
• suggestions
• spelling correction
• semantic matching
• keyboard navigation
• loading state
• empty state
• no-result suggestions
Example:
User types:
“labour lawyer del”
Suggestions:
Labour lawyers in Delhi
Employment lawyers in Delhi
PF compliance lawyers in Delhi
Labour law firms in Delhi
Do not make search feel like submitting a traditional form.
10. SEARCH RESULT TRANSITIONS
Search should preserve user context.
Example:
User applies:
Delhi
↓
Labour Law
↓
High Court
↓
Available Online
Then opens profile.
When they press back:
All filters must remain.
Do not reset the search.
Preserve:
• filters
• sorting
• page
• query
• scroll position where practical
11. FILTER SYSTEM
Filters must work as an actual query system.
Do not create disconnected frontend filter states.
Frontend:
filter
↓
API
↓
search engine/database
↓
results
Update URL state where appropriate so search results can be:
• shared
• bookmarked
• indexed when appropriate
Example:
/lawyers?city=delhi&practice=labour&court=delhi-high-court
12. FILTER UX
Desktop:
left side filtering
Mobile:
filter bottom sheet / full-screen sheet
Every filter should show:
selected count
clear option
apply action where necessary
Do not force users to scroll through 50 filters.
Group intelligently.
13. RESULT SKELETONS
Never show a blank page during loading.
Create skeleton states for:
• lawyer cards
• profiles
• firms
• dashboards
• tables
• search results
• judgments
• resources
Skeletons should match actual content dimensions to reduce layout shift.
14. LOADING EXPERIENCE
Every asynchronous operation must have an intentional state.
States:
IDLE
LOADING
SUCCESS
EMPTY
ERROR
RETRY
PARTIAL
OFFLINE
Do not leave the UI frozen.
15. BUTTON BEHAVIOR
Every button needs:
Default
Hover
Focus
Active
Disabled
Loading
Success
Error
For async buttons:
“Book consultation”
↓
“Processing…”
↓
“Confirmed”
or
“Unable to complete. Try again.”
Never allow double submission.
16. FORMS
Forms must be extremely polished.
Include:
• labels
• helper text
• validation
• error messages
• success states
• autosave where useful
• required indicators
• accessible error association
Validate:
client side
AND
server side.
Never trust client-side validation alone.
17. AUTOSAVE
Where appropriate:
Profile editing
Matter notes
Draft referrals
Draft documents
Contract editing
Resource creation
should have autosave.
Display:
Saved
Saving…
Saved 12 seconds ago
Do not make users wonder whether their work was saved.
18. UNSAVED CHANGES
If a user is leaving a page with unsaved changes:
warn them.
But do not annoy users when nothing changed.
19. ERROR HANDLING
Every page needs thoughtful errors.
Examples:
Search failure
“Something went wrong while searching.”
Then:
Retry
or
Return to search
Profile unavailable
“Profile unavailable.”
Document upload failure
“Upload failed. Your original file has not been modified.”
Payment failure
“Payment could not be completed.”
Never expose raw stack traces.
20. GLOBAL ERROR BOUNDARIES
Implement application-level error boundaries.
One broken component should NOT crash the entire website.
Handle:
• route errors
• API errors
• component rendering errors
• network failures
• timeout
• invalid data
21. OFFLINE / BAD NETWORK HANDLING
Users may access the platform on poor mobile internet.
Handle:
• slow requests
• retries
• timeouts
• cached public content
• interrupted uploads
• connection loss
Display meaningful feedback.
22. OPTIMISTIC UI
Use optimistic updates where appropriate.
Examples:
Like/save resource
Update preference
Mark notification read
Save filter
But never use optimism where data integrity is critical.
For payments, bookings and legal actions:
use authoritative server confirmation.
23. MICRO-INTERACTIONS
Add subtle interaction design.
Examples:
• profile image transitions
• search expansion
• filter chips
• hover states
• button feedback
• drawer transitions
• page transitions
• card hover
• toast notifications
• progress indicators
Animations should communicate state.
Do NOT animate everything.
Use motion purposefully.
24. REDUCED MOTION
Respect:
prefers-reduced-motion
Do not force animated transitions on users who request reduced motion.
25. ACCESSIBILITY
Target WCAG 2.2 AA.
This includes:
• keyboard navigation
• focus visibility
• target sizing
• labels
• semantic markup
• screen reader support
• logical tab order
• accessible dialogs
• accessible dropdowns
• accessible autocomplete
• accessible errors
• color contrast
WCAG 2.2 explicitly addresses focus visibility, target size, accessible authentication and other interaction concerns.
Never use color alone to communicate status.
Example:
Do not show only:
green = verified
Instead:
✓ Verified
26. DESIGN SYSTEM
Create a real design system.
Define:
Typography
Spacing
Colors
Borders
Radius
Elevation
Shadows
Icons
Buttons
Inputs
Dropdowns
Tabs
Cards
Tables
Modals
Drawers
Tooltips
Toast
Badges
Empty states
Skeletons
Error states
Use design tokens.
Do not hardcode dozens of unrelated values.
27. COMPONENT ARCHITECTURE
Create reusable components.
For example:
Button
Input
Select
SearchInput
FilterChip
FilterPanel
ProfileCard
LawyerCard
FirmCard
CourtBadge
VerificationBadge
ReviewCard
BookingCard
Calendar
DocumentUploader
Timeline
MatterCard
NotificationItem
DataTable
Modal
Drawer
Toast
EmptyState
ErrorState
Skeleton
Do not create five nearly-identical button components.
28. DESIGN TOKENS
Centralize:
color tokens
spacing
font sizes
line heights
radius
shadows
breakpoints
z-index
motion durations
container widths
This will make global refinement much easier.
29. VISUAL HIERARCHY
The legal platform should communicate:
TRUST
then
CLARITY
then
ACTION.
A user should immediately understand:
Who is this lawyer?
Can I trust the information?
What can I do?
Where do I go next?

Make profile pages extremely rich but not cluttered.
Hero:

Verification
Practice area
Location
Jurisdiction
Primary action
Then:

Courts
Professional background
Experience

Reviews

Locations
Related professionals
Do not dump every data field onto the user at once.

31. RELATED PROFESSIONALS
At the end of lawyer profiles show:
Similar professionals

Professionals available for related matters
This creates a connected ecosystem.
32. LAWYER → LAWYER CONNECTION
Create visible context such as:

Do not turn it into a social-media-style feed.

Every matter should understand:

Tasks
Appointments
Payments
Deadlines
Communications

34. CROSS-PAGE CONTEXT
When the user views:
Lawyer profile
the platform should already know:
practice area
location
court
related professionals
available consultations
related legal resources
Do not make every page feel isolated.
35. SMART EMPTY STATES
Do not use:
“No data found.”
Instead:

Try:
Delhi
NCR
Online consultation
Related practice area
Empty states should help users recover.
36. PERSONALIZATION
For logged-in users:
Remember:

saved resources
consultations
matters
preferred locations
recently viewed profiles
But make privacy controls clear.
37. “SAVE” FUNCTIONALITY
Allow users to save:

Searches

and
Saved searches.

39. NOTIFICATION CENTER

Documents

Verification
System

40. DEEP LINKING
Every important object should have a reliable URL.
Examples:
/lawyers/[id]
/law-firms/[id]
/matters/[id]
/referrals/[id]
/judgments/[id]
/resources/[slug]
This makes the application easier to navigate and integrate.
41. URL STATE
Important user state should be reflected in URLs when practical:
Search
Filters
Sorting
Pagination
Tabs
Public content filters
This improves:

back navigation
bookmarking

42. SEO ARCHITECTURE
Public profiles should be search-engine friendly.
Use:
server rendering / pre-rendering where appropriate
semantic HTML
metadata
OpenGraph
canonical URLs
structured data
sitemaps
breadcrumbs
internal linking.
Modern pre-rendering can help performance and SEO, while optimized image handling can reduce payload and layout shift.
43. PERFORMANCE IS A FEATURE
Do not wait until the end to optimize performance.
Target excellent Core Web Vitals.
Pay particular attention to:
LCP
INP
CLS
TTFB
JS bundle size
image payload
font payload
API latency
database query time
search latency
44. PERFORMANCE BUDGET
Establish budgets.
For example:
JavaScript
Images
Fonts
API latency
Initial HTML
Third-party scripts
Track them continuously.
If a developer introduces a massive dependency:
challenge it.
Do not add packages casually.
45. IMAGES
Optimize:
• dimensions
• compression
• responsive sizes
• modern formats
• lazy loading
• placeholders
Avoid loading a 4K lawyer photo into a 64px avatar.
Use framework image optimization capabilities where available. Next.js, for example, provides responsive sizing, lazy loading and layout-shift protection through its Image component.
46. FONTS
Do not load 10 font weights.
Use only required weights.
Prevent font-loading layout shifts.
47. ICONS
Use one coherent icon system.
Do not mix:
Font Awesome
Lucide
Material
random SVGs
unless there is a compelling reason.
48. MAP EXPERIENCE
If maps are used:
Do not load maps immediately on every search.
Lazy load expensive map functionality.
Desktop:
map can be persistent.
Mobile:
map can be a dedicated view.
49. DATABASE PERFORMANCE
Inspect every major query.
Look for:
N+1 queries
unnecessary joins
missing indexes
duplicate queries
large payloads
unbounded pagination
Create proper indexes.
Use:
cursor pagination
where appropriate.
50. SEARCH PERFORMANCE
Do not query millions of lawyers using inefficient SQL LIKE patterns.
Design an actual search strategy.
Evaluate:
PostgreSQL full-text search
OpenSearch
Elasticsearch
semantic search
hybrid search.
Explain the choice.
51. PAGINATION
Never load 10,000 lawyers into the browser.
Use:
pagination
cursor pagination
infinite loading where beneficial.
Keep accessibility in mind.
52. CACHING
Identify what should be cached.
Examples:
Public lawyer profiles
practice areas
locations
courts
resources
popular searches
static pages
Do NOT cache highly sensitive private data incorrectly.
53. AUTHENTICATION
Support:
email
password/passwordless depending on architecture
OTP where appropriate
MFA
social login where appropriate.
Authentication should be secure and accessible.
54. AUTHORIZATION
Implement server-side permission checks.
Example:
Public user
Lawyer
Firm Admin
Firm Member
Corporate Admin
Corporate Legal User
LPO Admin
Platform Admin
Super Admin
Never rely only on frontend route guards.
55. TENANT ISOLATION
For firms and companies:
Tenant A
must never access
Tenant B
data.
Test this deliberately.
Create automated isolation tests.
56. DOCUMENT MANAGEMENT
Document uploads need:
• file type validation
• file size limits
• virus/malware scanning
• metadata handling
• access controls
• secure URLs
• expiration
• versioning
Never publicly expose private legal documents.
57. DOCUMENT PREVIEW
Where appropriate:
PDF
DOCX
Images
should have preview.

58. FILE UPLOAD UX
Show:
Uploading 45%
Uploading 78%
Completed
Failed
Retry
For multiple files:

Do not freeze the page.

Design booking as a clear sequence.
STEP 1
Consultation type
STEP 2
Date
STEP 3
Time
STEP 4

STEP 5

STEP 6
Review
STEP 7

STEP 8
Confirmation
Do not force users through unnecessary steps.

Handle:

duplicate request

client cancels

date picker + slot list

Reviews should be attached to genuine interactions where the chosen legal model allows them.
Study proven review systems such as Avvo, which ties reviews to actual attorney/client experiences and excludes non-client parties under its guidelines.
Build:

moderation
report
response
status
audit history

Use factual signals such as:
Verified
Claimed

Firm verified
Professional profile complete
Do not invent scores.

modal

# 101. MOST IMPORTANT PRODUCT PRINCIPLE

Do not create a website that merely says:

“Find a lawyer.”

Create a system that understands:

WHO needs help

WHAT legal problem they have

WHERE it needs to be handled

WHICH jurisdiction applies

WHAT type of professional is appropriate

WHETHER the professional is verified

WHETHER the professional is available

WHETHER another lawyer should handle the matter

HOW the matter should be managed

HOW documents should be exchanged

HOW the client/company should track the matter

HOW the matter can be referred

HOW the matter can be resolved

HOW recurring legal work can be automated

That is the product differentiation.

6. Create the data model.

10. Create the UX flows.

12. Only then begin implementation.

Do not skip these stages.

# 103. CRITICAL REQUIREMENT

The final result should be designed to feel like:

### “The infrastructure layer for discovering, engaging, collaborating with and managing legal professionals.”

NOT:

### “A website containing a list of lawyers.”

Build the product around TRUST + DISCOVERY + JURISDICTION + CONSULTATION + COLLABORATION + LEGAL OPERATIONS.

The system should be capable of growing from an Indian advocate directory into an international legal-services technology platform without requiring a complete rewrite.

Start with India.

Start with advocate discovery and professional profiles.

Use the Bar Council ecosystem as the foundational data layer.

Then build the transaction, collaboration and SaaS layers around it.

# 17. LAWYER TO LAWYER REFERRAL SYSTEM

REFER A MATTER

• chooses jurisdiction
• chooses specialization
• adds urgency
• attaches documents

Lawyer B:

Then:

MATTER → REFERRAL → COLLABORATION → TRACKING

WHO needs help

The final result should be designed to feel like:

### “The infrastructure layer for discovering, engaging, collaborating with and managing legal professionals.”

NOT:

### “A website containing a list of lawyers.”

Build the product around TRUST + DISCOVERY + JURISDICTION + CONSULTATION + COLLABORATION + LEGAL OPERATIONS.

### REFERRAL NETWORK

Allow lawyers to refer matters to other lawyers.

### LEGAL OPERATIONS PLATFORM

Allow businesses to manage legal work, contracts and external counsel.

### LPO MARKETPLACE

Connect businesses with legal process outsourcing providers and specialists.

### LEGAL KNOWLEDGE PLATFORM

Provide judgments, legal resources, guides, templates and explainers.

### DISPUTE RESOLUTION PLATFORM

Support mediation and arbitration workflows.

### SAAS PLATFORM

Offer subscription-based legal technology.

# 2. VERY IMPORTANT: LEGAL AND ETHICAL FEASIBILITY FIRST

Before designing the commercial marketplace, conduct a detailed legal/regulatory analysis.

This is critical.

Research current Indian regulations governing:

• Bar Council of India
• Advocates Act
• BCI Rules
• Rule 36
• advertising restrictions
• solicitation restrictions
• online legal-service platforms
• intermediary liability
• legal fee disclosure
• advocate-client confidentiality
• client testimonials
• reviews
• anonymous reviews
• lead generation
• referral fees
• commissions
• payment processing
• legal marketplaces
• professional conduct
• data protection
• Digital Personal Data Protection Act
• consumer protection
• IT laws
• cybersecurity requirements
• electronic contracts
• electronic signatures
• mediation
• arbitration
• KYC

Also research relevant rules for other countries because the architecture must eventually support international expansion.

DO NOT assume a feature is legally permitted simply because Practo, Upwork or another marketplace does it.

Create a matrix:

| Feature | India Legal Position | Risk | Required Controls | Can Launch? |
| ------- | -------------------- | ---- | ----------------- | ----------- |

Explicitly classify features as:

• Allowed
• Potentially restricted
• Requires legal review
• Prohibited unless regulations change
• International-only
• Can be implemented in modified form

The product architecture must support compliance changes without rebuilding the entire system.

# 3. DATA SOURCE: BAR COUNCIL DATABASE

Use the Bar Council of India State Bar Council directory as a primary source for research and data architecture.

Reference:

https://www.barcouncilofindia.org/info/sbc

Delhi State Bar Council members reference:

https://www.barcouncilofindia.org/info/sbc-members/SBC05

The BCI website contains State Bar Council records and member information.

DO NOT simply copy data blindly.

Design a controlled data ingestion pipeline.

Research:

• BCI
• State Bar Councils
• publicly available official advocate databases
• other legally permissible public sources

Determine exactly what information is legally and technically permissible to ingest and display.

---

# 4. ADVOCATE DATA INGESTION SYSTEM

Build an automated data pipeline.

Architecture:

SOURCE
↓
CRAWLER
↓
RAW DATA STORAGE
↓
VALIDATION
↓
NORMALIZATION
↓
DEDUPLICATION
↓
ENTITY RESOLUTION
↓
VERIFICATION
↓
PROFILE CREATION
↓
SEARCH INDEX
↓
PUBLIC PROFILE

The system should support:

• scheduled crawling
• incremental updates
• change detection
• duplicate detection
• record versioning
• source attribution
• ingestion logs
• failed record queues
• retry mechanisms
• data provenance
• freshness timestamps
• administrator review
• opt-out/correction requests

Never expose scraped personal data merely because it is technically accessible.

Implement:

• robots.txt respect
• rate limiting
• source-specific crawling rules
• terms-of-use review
• data minimization
• privacy controls
• source attribution

# 17. LAWYER TO LAWYER REFERRAL SYSTEM

This is a major differentiator.

Example:

A Delhi High Court advocate gets a matter in Jabalpur.

They can search:

“Jabalpur High Court advocate”

and identify a suitable verified professional.

Create:

REFER A MATTER

workflow.

Lawyer A:

• creates referral request
• adds matter details
• chooses jurisdiction
• chooses specialization
• adds urgency
• attaches documents
• sends invitation

Lawyer B:

• receives referral
• reviews
• accepts
• declines
• requests information

Then:

MATTER → REFERRAL → COLLABORATION → TRACKING

Create permissions for:

• referring lawyer
• receiving lawyer
• client
• firm administrator

IMPORTANT:

Research and design this feature around professional conduct rules and prohibited fee-sharing/referral arrangements.

Do not assume commission-based referrals are permitted.

Create a system that understands:

WHO needs help

WHAT legal problem they have

WHERE it needs to be handled

WHICH jurisdiction applies

WHAT type of professional is appropriate

WHETHER the professional is verified

WHETHER the professional is available

WHETHER another lawyer should handle the matter

HOW the matter should be managed

HOW documents should be exchanged

HOW the matter can be referred

HOW the matter can be resolved

The final result should be designed to feel like:

### “The infrastructure layer for discovering, engaging, collaborating with and managing legal professionals.”

or

# 1. CORE PRODUCT VISION

# 2. VERY IMPORTANT: LEGAL AND ETHICAL FEASIBILITY FIRST

Before designing the commercial marketplace, conduct a detailed legal/regulatory analysis.

This is critical.

Research current Indian regulations governing:

• Bar Council of India
• Advocates Act
• BCI Rules
• Rule 36
• advertising restrictions
• solicitation restrictions
• online legal-service platforms
• intermediary liability
• legal fee disclosure
• advocate-client confidentiality
• client testimonials
• reviews
• anonymous reviews
• lead generation
• referral fees
• commissions
• payment processing
• legal marketplaces
• professional conduct
• data protection
• Digital Personal Data Protection Act
• consumer protection
• IT laws
• cybersecurity requirements
• electronic contracts
• electronic signatures
• mediation
• arbitration
• KYC

Also research relevant rules for other countries because the architecture must eventually support international expansion.

DO NOT assume a feature is legally permitted simply because Practo, Upwork or another marketplace does it.

Create a matrix:

| Feature | India Legal Position | Risk | Required Controls | Can Launch? |
| ------- | -------------------- | ---- | ----------------- | ----------- |

Explicitly classify features as:

• Allowed
• Potentially restricted
• Requires legal review
• Prohibited unless regulations change
• International-only
• Can be implemented in modified form

The product architecture must support compliance changes without rebuilding the entire system.

REFER A MATTER

workflow.

• chooses specialization
• adds urgency
• attaches documents

Lawyer B:

MATTER → REFERRAL → COLLABORATION → TRACKING

Search should preserve user context.
Example:
User applies:
Delhi
↓
Labour Law
↓
High Court
↓
Available Online
Then opens profile.
When they press back:
All filters must remain.
Do not reset the search.
Preserve:
• filters
• sorting
• page
• query
• scroll position where practical
11. FILTER SYSTEM
Filters must work as an actual query system.
Do not create disconnected frontend filter states.
Frontend:
filter
↓
API
↓
search engine/database
↓
results
Update URL state where appropriate so search results can be:
• shared
• bookmarked
• indexed when appropriate
Example:
/lawyers?city=delhi&practice=labour&court=delhi-high-court
12. FILTER UX
Desktop:
left side filtering
Mobile:
filter bottom sheet / full-screen sheet
Every filter should show:
selected count
clear option
apply action where necessary
Do not force users to scroll through 50 filters.
Group intelligently.
13. RESULT SKELETONS
Never show a blank page during loading.
Create skeleton states for:
• lawyer cards
• profiles
• firms
• dashboards
• tables
• search results
• judgments
• resources
Skeletons should match actual content dimensions to reduce layout shift.
14. LOADING EXPERIENCE
Every asynchronous operation must have an intentional state.
States:
IDLE
LOADING
SUCCESS
EMPTY
ERROR
RETRY
PARTIAL
OFFLINE
Do not leave the UI frozen.
15. BUTTON BEHAVIOR
Every button needs:
Default
Hover
Focus
Active
Disabled
Loading
Success
Error
For async buttons:
“Book consultation”
↓
“Processing…”
↓
“Confirmed”
or
“Unable to complete. Try again.”
Never allow double submission.
16. FORMS
Forms must be extremely polished.
Include:
• labels
• helper text
• validation
• error messages
• success states
• autosave where useful
• required indicators
• accessible error association
Validate:
client side
AND
server side.
Never trust client-side validation alone.
17. AUTOSAVE
Where appropriate:
Profile editing
Matter notes
Draft referrals
Draft documents
Contract editing
Resource creation
should have autosave.
Display:
Saved
Saving…
Saved 12 seconds ago
Do not make users wonder whether their work was saved.
18. UNSAVED CHANGES
If a user is leaving a page with unsaved changes:
warn them.
But do not annoy users when nothing changed.
19. ERROR HANDLING
Every page needs thoughtful errors.
Examples:
Search failure
“Something went wrong while searching.”
Then:
Retry
or
Return to search
Profile unavailable
“Profile unavailable.”
Document upload failure
“Upload failed. Your original file has not been modified.”
Payment failure
“Payment could not be completed.”
Never expose raw stack traces.
20. GLOBAL ERROR BOUNDARIES
Implement application-level error boundaries.
One broken component should NOT crash the entire website.
Handle:
• route errors
• API errors
• component rendering errors
• network failures
• timeout
• invalid data
21. OFFLINE / BAD NETWORK HANDLING
Users may access the platform on poor mobile internet.
Handle:
• slow requests
• retries
• timeouts
• cached public content
• interrupted uploads
• connection loss
Display meaningful feedback.
22. OPTIMISTIC UI
Use optimistic updates where appropriate.
Examples:
Like/save resource
Update preference
Mark notification read
Save filter
But never use optimism where data integrity is critical.
For payments, bookings and legal actions:
use authoritative server confirmation.
23. MICRO-INTERACTIONS
Add subtle interaction design.
Examples:
• profile image transitions
• search expansion
• filter chips
• hover states
• button feedback
• drawer transitions
• page transitions
• card hover
• toast notifications
• progress indicators
Animations should communicate state.
Do NOT animate everything.
Use motion purposefully.
24. REDUCED MOTION
Respect:
prefers-reduced-motion
Do not force animated transitions on users who request reduced motion.
25. ACCESSIBILITY
Target WCAG 2.2 AA.
This includes:
• keyboard navigation
• focus visibility
• target sizing
• labels
• semantic markup
• screen reader support
• logical tab order
• accessible dialogs
• accessible dropdowns
• accessible autocomplete
• accessible errors
• color contrast
WCAG 2.2 explicitly addresses focus visibility, target size, accessible authentication and other interaction concerns.
Never use color alone to communicate status.
Example:
Do not show only:
green = verified
Instead:
✓ Verified
26. DESIGN SYSTEM
Create a real design system.
Define:
Typography
Spacing
Colors
Borders
Radius
Elevation
Shadows
Icons
Buttons
Inputs
Dropdowns
Tabs
Cards
Tables
Modals
Drawers
Tooltips
Toast
Badges
Empty states
Skeletons
Error states
Use design tokens.
Do not hardcode dozens of unrelated values.
27. COMPONENT ARCHITECTURE
Create reusable components.
For example:
Button
Input
Select
SearchInput
FilterChip
FilterPanel
ProfileCard
LawyerCard
FirmCard
CourtBadge
VerificationBadge

Calendar

Drawer
Toast
EmptyState

Skeleton
Do not create five nearly-identical button components.
28. DESIGN TOKENS
Centralize:
color tokens
spacing
font sizes
line heights
radius
shadows
breakpoints
z-index
motion durations
container widths
This will make global refinement much easier.
29. VISUAL HIERARCHY
The legal platform should communicate:
TRUST
then
CLARITY
then
ACTION.
A user should immediately understand:
Who is this lawyer?
Can I trust the information?
What can I do?
Where do I go next?

Make profile pages extremely rich but not cluttered.

Location

Then:

At the end of lawyer profiles show:

Create visible context such as:

Tasks

Deadlines
Communications

34. CROSS-PAGE CONTEXT
When the user views:

the platform should already know:
practice area
location
court
related professionals
available consultations
related legal resources
Do not make every page feel isolated.
35. SMART EMPTY STATES
Do not use:
“No data found.”
Instead:

Try:
Delhi
NCR
Online consultation
Related practice area

36. PERSONALIZATION
For logged-in users:
Remember:
recent searches

saved resources
consultations
matters
preferred locations
recently viewed profiles
But make privacy controls clear.
37. “SAVE” FUNCTIONALITY

Searches

and
Saved searches.
38. SEARCH ALERTS

39. NOTIFICATION CENTER

Categories:
Bookings
Matters
Referrals
Messages
Documents

Verification
System

Unread

40. DEEP LINKING
Every important object should have a reliable URL.
Examples:
/lawyers/[id]
/law-firms/[id]
/matters/[id]
/referrals/[id]
/judgments/[id]
/resources/[slug]
This makes the application easier to navigate and integrate.
41. URL STATE
Important user state should be reflected in URLs when practical:
Search
Filters
Sorting
Pagination
Tabs
Public content filters
This improves:
sharing
back navigation
bookmarking
SEO
42. SEO ARCHITECTURE
Public profiles should be search-engine friendly.
Use:
server rendering / pre-rendering where appropriate
semantic HTML
metadata
OpenGraph
canonical URLs
structured data
sitemaps
breadcrumbs
internal linking.
Modern pre-rendering can help performance and SEO, while optimized image handling can reduce payload and layout shift.
43. PERFORMANCE IS A FEATURE
Do not wait until the end to optimize performance.
Target excellent Core Web Vitals.
Pay particular attention to:
LCP
INP
CLS
TTFB
JS bundle size
image payload
font payload
API latency
database query time
search latency
44. PERFORMANCE BUDGET
Establish budgets.
For example:
JavaScript
Images
Fonts
API latency
Initial HTML
Third-party scripts
Track them continuously.
If a developer introduces a massive dependency:
challenge it.
Do not add packages casually.
45. IMAGES
Optimize:
• dimensions
• compression
• responsive sizes
• modern formats
• lazy loading
• placeholders
Avoid loading a 4K lawyer photo into a 64px avatar.
Use framework image optimization capabilities where available. Next.js, for example, provides responsive sizing, lazy loading and layout-shift protection through its Image component.
46. FONTS
Do not load 10 font weights.
Use only required weights.
Prevent font-loading layout shifts.
47. ICONS
Use one coherent icon system.
Do not mix:
Font Awesome
Lucide
Material
random SVGs
unless there is a compelling reason.
48. MAP EXPERIENCE
If maps are used:
Do not load maps immediately on every search.
Lazy load expensive map functionality.
Desktop:
map can be persistent.
Mobile:
map can be a dedicated view.
49. DATABASE PERFORMANCE
Inspect every major query.
Look for:
N+1 queries
unnecessary joins
missing indexes
duplicate queries
large payloads
unbounded pagination
Create proper indexes.
Use:
cursor pagination
where appropriate.
50. SEARCH PERFORMANCE
Do not query millions of lawyers using inefficient SQL LIKE patterns.
Design an actual search strategy.
Evaluate:
PostgreSQL full-text search
OpenSearch
Elasticsearch
semantic search
hybrid search.
Explain the choice.
51. PAGINATION
Never load 10,000 lawyers into the browser.
Use:
pagination
cursor pagination
infinite loading where beneficial.
Keep accessibility in mind.
52. CACHING
Identify what should be cached.
Examples:
Public lawyer profiles
practice areas
locations
courts
resources
popular searches
static pages

53. AUTHENTICATION
Support:
email
password/passwordless depending on architecture
OTP where appropriate
MFA
social login where appropriate.

54. AUTHORIZATION
Implement server-side permission checks.
Example:
Public user
Lawyer
Firm Admin
Firm Member
Corporate Admin
Corporate Legal User
LPO Admin
Platform Admin
Super Admin
Never rely only on frontend route guards.
55. TENANT ISOLATION
For firms and companies:
Tenant A
must never access
Tenant B
data.
Test this deliberately.
Create automated isolation tests.
56. DOCUMENT MANAGEMENT

• file type validation
• file size limits
• virus/malware scanning
• metadata handling
• access controls
• secure URLs
• expiration
• versioning

Where appropriate:

DOCX

58. FILE UPLOAD UX

Uploading 78%
Completed
Failed

STEP 1

STEP 2

STEP 3

STEP 4

STEP 5

STEP 6

STEP 7

STEP 8

Do not force users through unnecessary steps.

response
status

Do not create a website that merely says:

“Find a lawyer.”

Create a system that understands:

WHO needs help

WHAT legal problem they have

WHERE it needs to be handled

WHICH jurisdiction applies

WHAT type of professional is appropriate

WHETHER the professional is verified

WHETHER the professional is available

WHETHER another lawyer should handle the matter

HOW the matter should be managed

HOW documents should be exchanged

HOW the client/company should track the matter

HOW the matter can be referred

HOW the matter can be resolved

HOW recurring legal work can be automated

That is the product differentiation.

# 103. CRITICAL REQUIREMENT

The final result should be designed to feel like:

### “The infrastructure layer for discovering, engaging, collaborating with and managing legal professionals.”

NOT:

### “A website containing a list of lawyers.”

Build the product around TRUST + DISCOVERY + JURISDICTION + CONSULTATION + COLLABORATION + LEGAL OPERATIONS.

The system should be capable of growing from an Indian advocate directory into an international legal-services technology platform without requiring a complete rewrite.

Start with India.

Start with advocate discovery and professional profiles.

Use the Bar Council ecosystem as the foundational data layer.

Then build the transaction, collaboration and SaaS layers around it.

CLAUDE CODE — EXTREME PRODUCT QUALITY + RESPONSIVENESS + INTERACTION + PRODUCTION READINESS PROMPT
IMPORTANT
You are NOT being asked to merely create a collection of pages.
You are being asked to create a fully functioning, interconnected, production-quality legal technology platform.
Treat this project as if:
• millions of users could eventually use it
• thousands/millions of lawyer profiles could exist
• law firms will depend on it
• companies will use it for legal operations
• sensitive legal documents will pass through it
• users will access it from phones, tablets and desktops
• search engines will index public pages
• users will expect the quality of Practo, Stripe, Apple, Linear and Bloomberg
Do not stop at visual appearance.
Everything must work.
Every button should have a purpose.
Every interaction should have a response.
Every page should connect logically to the rest of the system.
Every API state should be handled.
Every component must be responsive.
Every major flow must be testable.
1. FIRST: AUDIT THE EXISTING PROJECT
Before touching the code:
Inspect the complete repository.
Identify:
• framework
• frontend architecture
• backend architecture
• database
• components
• routes
• APIs
• authentication
• state management
• styling system
• design tokens
• assets
• environment variables
• third-party services
• existing technical debt
Create:
PROJECT_AUDIT.md
Include:
CURRENT STATE
PROBLEMS
DUPLICATIONS
BROKEN FLOWS
MISSING FEATURES
PERFORMANCE ISSUES
RESPONSIVENESS ISSUES
ACCESSIBILITY ISSUES
SECURITY ISSUES
ARCHITECTURAL PROBLEMS
RECOMMENDED TARGET STATE
Do NOT randomly rewrite working architecture.
Improve it deliberately.
2. DO NOT BUILD “STATIC MOCKUP SOFTWARE”
This is a critical instruction.
Do not create interfaces where:
button → nothing
search → fake result
filter → decorative UI
book appointment → fake popup
login → fake authentication
dashboard → static cards
review → fake submission
profile → hardcoded information
referral → nonfunctional modal
payment → placeholder
Every major action must either:

1. work,
2. connect to a real backend/API,
3. or have a clearly documented temporary mock layer that can be replaced without rewriting the frontend.

3. BUILD THE PLATFORM AS ONE CONNECTED SYSTEM
Think in relationships rather than pages.
For example:
LAWYER PROFILE
connects to
LAWYER ACCOUNT
connects to
VERIFICATION
connects to
PRACTICE AREAS
connects to
COURTS
connects to
LOCATIONS
connects to
AVAILABILITY
connects to
BOOKINGS
connects to
CONSULTATIONS
connects to
MATTERS
connects to
REFERRALS
connects to
REVIEWS
connects to
PAYMENTS
connects to
NOTIFICATIONS
connects to
ANALYTICS.
Everything should form a coherent product graph.

Create a global information architecture.
Everything must have predictable relationships.
For example:

Never create disconnected pages.
5. RESPONSIVE DESIGN IS A FIRST-CLASS REQUIREMENT
Do NOT build desktop first and “make it responsive later.”
Design responsively from the beginning.
The platform must work across:
• 320px phones
• 375px phones
• 390px phones
• 414px phones
• tablets
• laptops
• 1440px desktops
• 1920px displays
• large professional monitors
Use fluid layouts.
Use flexible grids.
Use container queries where appropriate.
Do not rely entirely on arbitrary breakpoint overrides.
6. RESPONSIVENESS TESTING
Test every major screen at:
320px
375px
390px
414px
768px
834px
1024px
1280px
1440px
1920px
Create an automated responsive test matrix.
Look for:
• overflow
• clipped text
• broken buttons
• broken cards
• horizontal scrolling
• modal overflow
• unreadable tables
• nav collisions
• images stretching
• unexpected whitespace
• inaccessible controls
Fix the ROOT component rather than adding random CSS hacks.
7. MOBILE IS NOT A SHRUNK DESKTOP
This is extremely important.
Mobile should have its own interaction strategy.
For example:
Desktop:
Search + filters + results + map
Mobile:
Search
↓
Filter button
↓
Bottom sheet filters
↓
Results
Similarly:
Desktop navigation:
full navigation
Mobile:
compact header
search
profile
notifications
menu
Use mobile-specific interaction patterns when they improve usability.
8. NAVIGATION EXPERIENCE
Create:
• sticky navigation where useful
• scroll-aware header
• proper mobile navigation
• breadcrumbs
• contextual navigation
• back navigation
• active states
• keyboard navigation
Never trap the user inside a flow.
The user should always understand:
Where am I?
How did I get here?
What can I do next?
How do I go back?
9. SEARCH EXPERIENCE MUST FEEL INSTANT
Search is one of the most important product interactions.
Implement:
• autocomplete
• recent searches
• popular searches
• suggestions
• spelling correction
• semantic matching
• keyboard navigation
• loading state
• empty state
• no-result suggestions
Example:
User types:
“labour lawyer del”
Suggestions:
Labour lawyers in Delhi
Employment lawyers in Delhi
PF compliance lawyers in Delhi
Labour law firms in Delhi
Do not make search feel like submitting a traditional form.
10. SEARCH RESULT TRANSITIONS
Search should preserve user context.
Example:
User applies:
Delhi
↓
Labour Law
↓
High Court
↓
Available Online
Then opens profile.
When they press back:
All filters must remain.
Do not reset the search.
Preserve:
• filters
• sorting
• page
• query
• scroll position where practical
11. FILTER SYSTEM
Filters must work as an actual query system.
Do not create disconnected frontend filter states.
Frontend:
filter
↓
API
↓
search engine/database
↓
results
Update URL state where appropriate so search results can be:
• shared
• bookmarked
• indexed when appropriate
Example:
/lawyers?city=delhi&practice=labour&court=delhi-high-court
12. FILTER UX
Desktop:
left side filtering
Mobile:
filter bottom sheet / full-screen sheet
Every filter should show:
selected count
clear option
apply action where necessary
Do not force users to scroll through 50 filters.
Group intelligently.
13. RESULT SKELETONS
Never show a blank page during loading.
Create skeleton states for:
• lawyer cards
• profiles
• firms
• dashboards
• tables
• search results
• judgments
• resources
Skeletons should match actual content dimensions to reduce layout shift.
14. LOADING EXPERIENCE
Every asynchronous operation must have an intentional state.
States:
IDLE
LOADING
SUCCESS
EMPTY
ERROR
RETRY
PARTIAL
OFFLINE
Do not leave the UI frozen.
15. BUTTON BEHAVIOR
Every button needs:
Default
Hover
Focus
Active
Disabled
Loading
Success
Error
For async buttons:
“Book consultation”
↓
“Processing…”
↓
“Confirmed”
or
“Unable to complete. Try again.”
Never allow double submission.
16. FORMS
Forms must be extremely polished.
Include:
• labels
• helper text
• validation
• error messages
• success states
• autosave where useful
• required indicators
• accessible error association
Validate:
client side
AND
server side.
Never trust client-side validation alone.
17. AUTOSAVE
Where appropriate:
Profile editing
Matter notes
Draft referrals
Draft documents
Contract editing
Resource creation
should have autosave.
Display:
Saved
Saving…
Saved 12 seconds ago
Do not make users wonder whether their work was saved.
18. UNSAVED CHANGES
If a user is leaving a page with unsaved changes:
warn them.
But do not annoy users when nothing changed.
19. ERROR HANDLING
Every page needs thoughtful errors.
Examples:
Search failure
“Something went wrong while searching.”
Then:
Retry
or
Return to search
Profile unavailable
“Profile unavailable.”
Document upload failure
“Upload failed. Your original file has not been modified.”
Payment failure
“Payment could not be completed.”
Never expose raw stack traces.
20. GLOBAL ERROR BOUNDARIES
Implement application-level error boundaries.
One broken component should NOT crash the entire website.
Handle:
• route errors
• API errors
• component rendering errors
• network failures
• timeout
• invalid data
21. OFFLINE / BAD NETWORK HANDLING
Users may access the platform on poor mobile internet.
Handle:
• slow requests
• retries
• timeouts
• cached public content
• interrupted uploads
• connection loss
Display meaningful feedback.
22. OPTIMISTIC UI
Use optimistic updates where appropriate.
Examples:
Like/save resource
Update preference
Mark notification read
Save filter
But never use optimism where data integrity is critical.
For payments, bookings and legal actions:
use authoritative server confirmation.
23. MICRO-INTERACTIONS
Add subtle interaction design.
Examples:
• profile image transitions
• search expansion
• filter chips
• hover states
• button feedback
• drawer transitions
• page transitions
• card hover
• toast notifications
• progress indicators
Animations should communicate state.
Do NOT animate everything.
Use motion purposefully.
24. REDUCED MOTION
Respect:
prefers-reduced-motion
Do not force animated transitions on users who request reduced motion.
25. ACCESSIBILITY
Target WCAG 2.2 AA.
This includes:
• keyboard navigation
• focus visibility
• target sizing
• labels
• semantic markup
• screen reader support
• logical tab order
• accessible dialogs
• accessible dropdowns
• accessible autocomplete
• accessible errors
• color contrast
WCAG 2.2 explicitly addresses focus visibility, target size, accessible authentication and other interaction concerns.
Never use color alone to communicate status.
Example:
Do not show only:
green = verified
Instead:
✓ Verified

The legal platform should communicate:

then

Public profiles should be search-engine friendly.
Use:

metadata

43. PERFORMANCE IS A FEATURE
Do not wait until the end to optimize performance.
Target excellent Core Web Vitals.
Pay particular attention to:
LCP
INP
CLS
TTFB
JS bundle size
image payload
font payload
API latency
database query time
search latency
44. PERFORMANCE BUDGET
Establish budgets.
For example:
JavaScript
Images
Fonts
API latency
Initial HTML
Third-party scripts
Track them continuously.
If a developer introduces a massive dependency:
challenge it.
Do not add packages casually.
45. IMAGES
Optimize:
• dimensions
• compression
• responsive sizes
• modern formats
• lazy loading
• placeholders
Avoid loading a 4K lawyer photo into a 64px avatar.
Use framework image optimization capabilities where available. Next.js, for example, provides responsive sizing, lazy loading and layout-shift protection through its Image component.
46. FONTS
Do not load 10 font weights.
Use only required weights.
Prevent font-loading layout shifts.
47. ICONS
Use one coherent icon system.
Do not mix:
Font Awesome
Lucide
Material
random SVGs
unless there is a compelling reason.
48. MAP EXPERIENCE
If maps are used:
Do not load maps immediately on every search.
Lazy load expensive map functionality.
Desktop:
map can be persistent.
Mobile:
map can be a dedicated view.
49. DATABASE PERFORMANCE
Inspect every major query.
Look for:
N+1 queries
unnecessary joins
missing indexes
duplicate queries
large payloads
unbounded pagination
Create proper indexes.
Use:
cursor pagination
where appropriate.
50. SEARCH PERFORMANCE
Do not query millions of lawyers using inefficient SQL LIKE patterns.
Design an actual search strategy.
Evaluate:
PostgreSQL full-text search
OpenSearch
Elasticsearch
semantic search
hybrid search.
Explain the choice.
51. PAGINATION
Never load 10,000 lawyers into the browser.
Use:
pagination
cursor pagination
infinite loading where beneficial.
Keep accessibility in mind.
52. CACHING
Identify what should be cached.
Examples:
Public lawyer profiles
practice areas
locations
courts
resources
popular searches
static pages
Do NOT cache highly sensitive private data incorrectly.
53. AUTHENTICATION
Support:
email
password/passwordless depending on architecture
OTP where appropriate
MFA
social login where appropriate.
Authentication should be secure and accessible.
54. AUTHORIZATION
Implement server-side permission checks.
Example:
Public user
Lawyer
Firm Admin
Firm Member
Corporate Admin
Corporate Legal User
LPO Admin
Platform Admin
Super Admin
Never rely only on frontend route guards.
55. TENANT ISOLATION
For firms and companies:
Tenant A
must never access
Tenant B
data.
Test this deliberately.
Create automated isolation tests.

Document uploads need:
• file type validation

• versioning

# CLAUDE CODE — TOKEN SAVER MODE

## PRIMARY OBJECTIVE

Operate in **high-efficiency / low-token mode** while continuing to work like a senior autonomous engineering agent.

Do NOT sacrifice:

• correctness
• testing
• security
• responsiveness
• design quality
• architecture
• functionality

Instead, reduce unnecessary:

• explanations
• repeated file reads
• repeated searches
• repeated code output
• repeated summaries
• redundant tool calls
• verbose reasoning
• duplicate implementation

The goal is:

**MAXIMUM ACTUAL WORK + MINIMUM TOKEN CONSUMPTION**

---

# 1. DO THE WORK, DON'T EXPLAIN THE WORK

Prefer:

INSPECT → FIX → TEST

instead of:

INSPECT → EXPLAIN → ASK → EXPLAIN → FIX.

Do not narrate obvious operations.

Do not give long progress reports.

Only report:

• important discoveries
• blockers
• architectural decisions
• completed milestones
• failures requiring attention

---

# 2. BATCH TOOL CALLS

Whenever possible, group related inspections into one operation.

For example, instead of reading:

10 files individually

inspect:

the relevant directory structure

and targeted files together.

Batch:

• file inspection
• searches
• test execution
• status checks
• related documentation research

Avoid unnecessary sequential tool calls.

---

# 3. DO NOT REREAD FILES UNNECESSARILY

Before opening a file:

ask:

“Have I already seen enough of this file?”

If yes:

do not reread it.

Maintain a mental/project-context summary of:

• architecture
• important routes
• key components
• database schema
• APIs
• configuration
• design system

---

# 4. USE TARGETED SEARCH

Do not scan the entire repository repeatedly.

Search specifically for:

routes

components

API calls

database models

TODO

mock

placeholder

broken imports

hardcoded data

unused dependencies

relevant feature names.

Use focused searches.

---

# 5. PRIORITIZE HIGH-VALUE FILES

Inspect first:

package.json

Docker files

environment configuration

main app entry

routing

database schema

API entry points

design system

global CSS

layout

authentication

search

core profile components.

Do not waste tokens reading unrelated files.

---

# 6. MAINTAIN A COMPACT PROJECT MEMORY

Create/update:

`CLAUDE_PROJECT_STATE.md`

Keep it concise.

Include only:

### ARCHITECTURE

Current frontend/backend/database structure.

### ACTIVE TASK

What is being fixed now.

### COMPLETED

Completed major changes.

### KNOWN ISSUES

Remaining high-priority issues.

### IMPORTANT FILES

Key files and their purpose.

### DECISIONS

Important architectural decisions.

### TEST STATUS

Passing/failing critical tests.

Update this file instead of repeatedly rediscovering the same information.

---

# 7. USE CHECKPOINTS

Work in milestones.

Example:

CHECKPOINT 1
Application runs

CHECKPOINT 2
Core navigation works

CHECKPOINT 3
Search works

CHECKPOINT 4
Profiles work

CHECKPOINT 5
Booking works

CHECKPOINT 6
Responsive design works

CHECKPOINT 7
QA complete

After each checkpoint:

update the compact project state.

---

# 8. DON'T REWRITE GOOD CODE

Before modifying:

inspect

understand

then patch.

Prefer:

small targeted changes

over:

rewriting entire files.

Do not regenerate components unnecessarily.

---

# 9. DON'T DUPLICATE COMPONENTS

Before creating a component:

search the project.

If an equivalent component exists:

reuse or extend it.

Do not create:

Button2

ButtonNew

ProfileCardNew

MobileProfileCard

unless there is a genuine architectural need.

---

# 10. USE THE EXISTING DESIGN SYSTEM

Before adding styles:

inspect existing tokens.

Reuse:

colors

spacing

typography

radii

shadows

breakpoints.

Only introduce new tokens when necessary.

---

# 11. FIX ROOT CAUSES

If 20 pages have incorrect spacing:

DO NOT patch 20 pages individually.

Fix:

container

spacing token

layout primitive

component.

Prefer systemic fixes.

---

# 12. BATCH UI FIXES

When several screens have the same issue:

fix the shared component once.

Examples:

wrong button height

incorrect card radius

bad mobile padding

misaligned headings

broken focus states.

---

# 13. DON'T OVERDESCRIBE IMPLEMENTATION

When changing code, do not produce long textual explanations.

Use brief notes such as:

“Fixed shared card spacing across profile/search/dashboard.”

Not:

a 500-word explanation of CSS methodology.

---

# 14. TEST SMARTLY

Do not run the entire test suite after every tiny change.

Use:

targeted test

↓

fix

↓

targeted test

Then run:

full test suite

at milestone boundaries.

---

# 15. TEST FAILURE TRIAGE

When tests fail:

group related failures.

Example:

15 failures caused by:

shared Button component.

Fix Button once.

Then rerun affected tests.

Do not debug each symptom independently.

---

# 16. USE BROWSER TESTS INTELLIGENTLY

Do not screenshot every page after every modification.

Capture:

baseline

major milestone

final regression.

During development:

test only the affected routes.

---

# 17. RESPONSIVE TESTING

Do not test every viewport after every CSS change.

Use a representative matrix:

Mobile: 390px

Tablet: 768px

Desktop: 1440px

Then perform final full viewport testing.

---

# 18. PERFORMANCE TESTING

Do not repeatedly run expensive performance analysis during tiny changes.

Run:

development checks

then

milestone performance audit

then

final performance audit.

---

# 19. RESEARCH EFFICIENTLY

When researching online:

prefer authoritative sources.

First search:

official documentation

standards

primary sources.

Avoid opening dozens of redundant articles.

Use one strong source instead of five weak ones where possible.

---

# 20. DO NOT RESEARCH WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN

Before researching:

check the existing project documentation.

Only research unresolved questions.

---

# 21. DATA INGESTION EFFICIENCY

For external/public data:

do not repeatedly download unchanged data.

Use:

cache

hash/checksum

last-modified

ETag where available

incremental crawling

change detection.

---

# 22. SCRAPING EFFICIENCY

Use:

rate limiting

pagination tracking

checkpointing

retry with backoff

deduplication.

If a page has already been processed:

do not process it again unless it changed.

Respect robots.txt, source terms and technical access controls.

Do not bypass authentication, CAPTCHAs or other access restrictions.

---

# 23. STORE RAW DATA ONCE

Pipeline:

RAW

↓

NORMALIZED

↓

VALIDATED

↓

PUBLISHED

Do not repeatedly scrape the same source just to regenerate normalized records.

---

# 24. ASSET EFFICIENCY

Before downloading an asset:

check whether it already exists locally.

Avoid duplicate:

images

icons

logos

fonts.

Maintain:

`ASSET_MANIFEST.md`

---

# 25. DO NOT GENERATE UNNECESSARY ASSETS

Do not create decorative images simply to fill space.

Only create/download assets that improve:

brand

UX

content

performance.

---

# 26. KEEP RESPONSES COMPACT

When reporting progress:

use concise structure:

DONE:
Search fixed
Responsive profile fixed
Docker build fixed

NEXT:
Booking flow
Accessibility

BLOCKER:
Payment provider credentials unavailable

Do not provide long prose.

---

# 27. AVOID REPETITIVE STATUS UPDATES

Do not repeatedly say:

“I inspected…”

“I checked…”

“I am now…”

Only report meaningful changes.

---

# 28. DON'T ASK FOR PERMISSION FOR OBVIOUS SAFE ACTIONS

When an issue can be safely diagnosed and fixed:

fix it.

Do not ask:

“Should I inspect the CSS?”

“Should I run Docker?”

“Should I test mobile?”

Do it.

---

# 29. DON'T ASK QUESTIONS THAT CAN BE ANSWERED FROM THE PROJECT

Inspect the repository, configuration and documentation first.

Only ask when an external business decision is genuinely required.

---

# 30. USE EXISTING DEPENDENCIES

Before installing a new package:

check package.json.

If the capability already exists:

reuse it.

Avoid dependency bloat.

---

# 31. AVOID LARGE CODE OUTPUT IN CHAT

Do not dump huge files into the response.

Make changes directly in the project.

Report:

what changed

where

why

test result.

---

# 32. KEEP DOCUMENTATION COMPRESSED

Documentation should be:

clear

structured

compact.

Avoid repeating the same architecture explanation across five files.

Cross-reference instead.

---

# 33. ONE SOURCE OF TRUTH

For:

design tokens

environment variables

API types

database enums

roles

permissions

practice areas

courts

locations

statuses

maintain a single authoritative source.

---

# 34. DON'T DUPLICATE BUSINESS LOGIC

If logic exists in:

backend/service layer

do not recreate the same rules separately in multiple frontend components.

---

# 35. CACHE EXPENSIVE OPERATIONS

Where safe, cache:

public profiles

locations

courts

practice areas

static resources

search metadata.

Do not cache sensitive private matter data incorrectly.

---

# 36. AVOID PREMATURE OPTIMIZATION

First measure.

Then optimize the actual bottleneck.

Do not spend tokens optimizing hypothetical problems.

---

# 37. ERROR HANDLING SHOULD BE CENTRALIZED

Create reusable:

error handling

API response handling

logging

notification

validation

patterns.

Do not reinvent them on every page.

---

# 38. CONSOLIDATE REPETITIVE CSS

If the same CSS pattern appears repeatedly:

create a reusable utility/component/token.

Do not copy large style blocks.

---

# 39. USE AUTOMATION FOR REPETITIVE FIXES

If 100 files need the same mechanical change:

use a script/codemod.

Do not manually edit 100 files.

---

# 40. VERIFY AFTER BULK CHANGES

After scripted changes:

run:

format

lint

typecheck

targeted tests.

Then inspect representative affected screens.

---

# 41. PRIORITY MODEL

Always prioritize:

P0 = broken/security/data-loss

P1 = core user journey

P2 = responsive/accessibility/performance

P3 = visual polish

P4 = nice-to-have.

Do not spend tokens polishing P4 while P0/P1 problems remain.

---

# 42. WORK FROM THE USER JOURNEY

When choosing what to inspect next:

prioritize:

Homepage

Search

Lawyer Profile

Booking

Referral

Matter

Dashboard

These are the product's critical path.

---

# 43. TOKEN-SAVING RESEARCH FORMAT

When researching something:

collect only:

Decision

Reason

Source

Implementation impact.

Do not produce long essays internally.

---

# 44. TOKEN-SAVING CODE REVIEW

For each file:

identify only:

critical bug

architecture issue

security issue

performance issue

UX issue.

Fix those first.

---

# 45. TOKEN-SAVING LOG REVIEW

Do not dump entire logs.

Search/filter for:

ERROR

WARN

FAIL

timeout

exception

critical patterns.

Inspect surrounding lines only when needed.

---

# 46. TOKEN-SAVING DATABASE REVIEW

Do not dump the complete database.

Inspect:

schema

relations

indexes

slow queries

critical entities.

---

# 47. TOKEN-SAVING API REVIEW

Generate a concise endpoint inventory:

METHOD

ROUTE

PURPOSE

AUTH

STATUS.

Only inspect implementation deeply when the endpoint is relevant to a failing workflow.

---

# 48. TOKEN-SAVING UI REVIEW

Use a defect matrix:

PAGE | ISSUE | SEVERITY | FIX

Do not produce verbose descriptions for every pixel.

---

# 49. VISUAL QA

For screenshots:

compare against:

spacing

alignment

hierarchy

responsiveness

consistency

brand.

Record only actionable defects.

---

# 50. FINAL CLEANUP

Before completion:

remove unnecessary logs

remove temporary scripts

remove debug UI

remove screenshots created only for testing

remove unused packages

remove dead code

unless needed for documentation.

---

# 51. IMPORTANT: NEVER TRADE QUALITY FOR TOKENS

Token saver mode means:

LESS TALK

LESS REDUNDANCY

SMARTER TOOL USAGE

BETTER BATCHING

NOT:

LESS TESTING

LESS SECURITY

LESS DESIGN QUALITY

LESS FUNCTIONALITY

LESS QA.

---

# 52. FINAL COMMAND

Operate as an autonomous senior engineer.

Use the repository as the source of truth.

Use tools efficiently.

Batch work.

Cache knowledge.

Avoid rereading files.

Fix systemic problems at their source.

Test intelligently.

Research only when needed.

Keep written communication compact.

Spend tokens on:

**BUILDING**

**FIXING**

**TESTING**

**VERIFYING**

rather than explaining obvious actions.

The objective is:

### MINIMUM TOKEN WASTE

### MAXIMUM REAL WORK

### ZERO UNNECESSARY REPETITION

### PRODUCTION-GRADE RESULT

Yes. For your platform, do not make “Legal Matters” just a flat list of 20 categories. You need a comprehensive India Legal Matter Taxonomy that can drive search, lawyer profiles, filters, intake, referrals, SEO pages, LPO services, corporate requests and matching.
I’ve expanded it substantially and cross checked the breadth against Indian government/legal sources. For example, Department of Justice material specifically identifies matrimonial/family disputes, criminal matters, land acquisition, labour, workmen compensation, bank recovery, pension, housing, consumer, electricity, telephone and municipal matters as recurring legal-service areas. The official tribunal framework also spans areas such as income tax, customs/excise, labour, administrative matters, railway claims, securities, debt recovery, telecom, company law, consumer disputes and electricity.

92. CRITICAL PRODUCT RECOMMENDATION
Do not put all these 90+ categories into one giant dropdown.
Create a hierarchy:
LEVEL 1 — LEGAL DOMAIN
Example:
Labour & Employment
LEVEL 2 — PRACTICE AREA
PF / ESI
LEVEL 3 — MATTER
PF contribution dispute
LEVEL 4 — SERVICE
Consultation / Notice / Representation / Litigation / Compliance
LEVEL 5 — FORUM
EPFO / Labour Court / CGIT / High Court etc.
LEVEL 6 — JURISDICTION
Country → State → District → City → Court
That gives you an extremely powerful matching engine.
For example:
User says:
“My employer hasn't deposited my PF in Delhi.”
The platform could map:
Domain: Labour & Employment
Practice: PF / EPF
Matter: PF contribution dispute
Service: Consultation / Representation
Jurisdiction: Delhi
Forum: EPFO / appropriate adjudicatory forum
Professional: Labour / Employment lawyer
Another:
User says:
“My electricity company has sent me a huge wrong bill.”
The system maps:
Domain: Electricity & Energy
Matter: Electricity billing dispute
Issue: Excess/wrong billing
Service: Consumer complaint / regulatory representation / litigation
Location: relevant state
Forum: appropriate electricity grievance/regulatory/consumer forum
This hierarchy is much better than simply having “Electricity Lawyer” as a category.
The official legal ecosystem itself spans courts, commissions and specialised tribunals across tax, labour, companies, debt recovery, consumer, electricity, telecom and securities, so your taxonomy should represent both the legal problem and the forum/jurisdiction rather than treating them as the same thing.
Recommended database structure

```
LEGAL_DOMAIN
```

    ↓
PRACTICE_AREA
    ↓
LEGAL_MATTER
    ↓
LEGAL_ISSUE
    ↓
LEGAL_SERVICE
    ↓
FORUM / TRIBUNAL
    ↓
COURT
    ↓
JURISDICTION
    ↓
LAWYER / LAW FIRM
This structure will make your platform much stronger for search, lawyer matching, AI intake, referrals, SEO, corporate legal requests and future international expansion.

5. IMPORTANT RENT AGREEMENT SYSTEM
Do NOT make one generic rent agreement.
Build:
COUNTRY
→ STATE
→ CITY
→ PROPERTY TYPE
→ RESIDENTIAL / COMMERCIAL
→ RENTAL TYPE
→ JURISDICTIONAL TEMPLATE
→ VERSION
Example:
India
→ Maharashtra
→ Mumbai
→ Residential
→ Leave & License
Another:
India
→ Uttar Pradesh
→ Noida
→ Residential
→ Tenancy
The reason is that tenancy rules and registration requirements vary between jurisdictions. Maharashtra, for example, contains a specific compulsory-registration provision for leave-and-license/letting agreements, while Uttar Pradesh has its own tenancy legislation and prescribed tenancy-agreement framework.
Never present a generic national template as universally valid.

# CLAUDE CODE — COMPLETE PROJECT RECONCILIATION, CONNECTIVITY, FUNCTIONALITY, UX AND REQUIREMENT AUDIT

## MISSION

You are now responsible for performing a **complete forensic audit, reconciliation and enhancement of the existing legal technology platform**.

Do NOT assume the project is complete.

Do NOT assume the visible UI represents the actual functionality.

Do NOT assume backend, frontend, database, assets, APIs, routes and workflows are connected.

Your job is to discover what actually exists, compare it against what was intended, identify everything missing or broken, establish the correct relationships, and then implement the missing pieces.

The final result must be:

**SIMPLE**

**FAST**

**EASY TO NAVIGATE**

**FULLY CONNECTED**

**FULLY FUNCTIONAL**

**RESPONSIVE**

**PREMIUM**

**TRUSTWORTHY**

**INTERNATIONAL-QUALITY**

The design philosophy should take inspiration from the simplicity of Practo's discovery experience, NOT copy its visual design or proprietary implementation. Practo's core user flow makes finding professionals, viewing relevant information and booking appointments straightforward, with availability and practitioner information exposed directly in the discovery experience.

---

# 1. ABSOLUTE RULE

Do not merely report problems.

**FIND THEM → CREATE TASKS → FIX THEM → TEST THEM → VERIFY THEM**

If something intended is missing:

ADD IT.

If something exists but is disconnected:

CONNECT IT.

If something exists but is broken:

FIX IT.

If something exists but is confusing:

REDESIGN IT.

If something exists but creates unnecessary complexity:

SIMPLIFY IT.

If a requirement is represented only visually but has no real functionality:

IMPLEMENT THE FUNCTIONALITY.

---

# 2. FIRST: SCAN THE ENTIRE PROJECT

Before changing anything, recursively inspect the entire repository.

Scan:

• every folder
• every source file
• every route
• every component
• every API
• every database schema/model
• every migration
• every configuration file
• every Docker file
• every environment/configuration reference
• every image
• every icon
• every font
• every document
• every JSON/CSV data file
• every test
• every script
• every utility
• every middleware
• every service
• every worker
• every seed
• every scraper/ingestion script
• every documentation file

Do not selectively inspect only the frontend.

The audit must cover:

FRONTEND

BACKEND

DATABASE

DATA

INFRASTRUCTURE

DESIGN

ASSETS

SECURITY

TESTING

SEO

AUTOMATION

DOCUMENTATION.

# 7. DON'T CONFUSE “VISIBLE” WITH “FUNCTIONAL”

For every major feature ask:

### Is it present?

### Is it visible?

### Is it clickable?

### Does the click perform an action?

### Does the frontend call the backend?

### Does the backend process it?

### Does the database persist it?

### Does the user see the resulting state?

### Is the action permission-controlled?

### Does the action generate notifications where required?

### Is it tested?

A feature is NOT COMPLETE until the entire chain works.

# 64. PRACTO SIMPLICITY PRINCIPLE

The lesson to take from Practo is not branding.

The lesson is:

**MAKE THE CORE JOB OBVIOUS.**

A user can:

search

see relevant professionals

understand the professional

see availability

book.

Practo explicitly describes search around specialty/location and booking, and its booking system exposes real-time appointment availability.

Our equivalent should be:

search legal problem/location

↓

see relevant professionals

↓

understand professional

↓

see jurisdiction/practice/verification

↓

request consultation

↓

book where available

↓

manage matter.
